title: P0 hostedAPI stream churn + memory pressure retro
summary: On 2029-12-12 at ~11:04 UTC we observed a P0 impact to the hosted API streaming surface: sustained client streaming stalls and elevated p50/p95 TTFB for streaming sessions in us-west-2. The user-facing symptoms were stalled streaming responses (no token traffic) and connection reconnects. The incident lasted ~62 minutes for the bulk of traffic before controlled mitigation, with complete cleanup following autoscaler and cache tuning over the next 3 hours.
impact: Approximately 18% of streaming sessions in us-west-2 experienced stalls lasting 10–45s; overall hosted streaming error-rate spiked from baseline 0.02% to 1.8% during the window. A subset of high-throughput partners saw multiple reconnects and increased token costs due to repeated replays. No data loss was detected; requests eventually resumed or were retried by clients.
timeline:
11:02 UTC — minor uptick in ephemeral connection churn detected by edge metrics
11:04 UTC — synthetic streaming check alerts (SRE-runbook) for elevated TTFB and stall count
11:07 UTC — oncall paged; initial hypothesis: edge TLS session churn or upstream edge autoscaler thrash
11:12 UTC — SREs observe high memory RSS on stream router processes consuming >85% of host memory on affected boxes
11:20 UTC — KV cache eviction rate spikes; many misses for hot prefixes correlated with memory pressure windows
11:28 UTC — memory pressure led to GC pauses and the stream muxer thread entering backpressure; token emission halted for affected sessions
11:34 UTC — mitigation: scaled router pool + force-evict large prefix caches on a subset of hosts to relieve memory spikes (quick rollback enabled)
11:45 UTC — observed decrease in stall count; p95 TTFB trending down but still above baseline
12:10 UTC — deployed hotfix: reduce per-session in-memory buffer cap and enable aggressive kv-prefetch throttle for streaming path (canary then rollout)
12:55 UTC — majority of sessions returned to normal; incident declared mitigated at 12:06 UTC for core traffic, full cleanup by 14:30 UTC
Note: timeline combines automated telemetry with manual investigator timestamps; some minor alarm jitter in logs due to retry storms.
detection_and_alerting:
Detection: synthetic streaming healthcheck alert triggered first (SRE-synthetic-streaming-p50-ttfb). Edge telemetry faceted by client id showed reconnection clusters. Automated alerting threshold was tuned for p95 > 800ms; this incident crossed that within 2m.
Gaps: there was no alert directly correlating high kv-cache eviction rate to streaming stalls. The memory RSS alerts were present but suppressed on some hosts due to earlier tuning to reduce alert noise.
root_cause:
Primary root cause: a regression in recent router-side memory accounting (merge of PR #4392) changed the logic that bounds per-session buffer allocations under slow-consumer conditions. Under a burst of high-concurrency streaming sessions with uneven prefix locality, the combined effect was: unbounded per-session buffers + increased KV cache churn for hot prefixes -> host memory pressure -> long GC pauses and stream muxer/backpressure cascades that stopped token emission.
Secondary contributor: the KV cache prefetch throttle was permissive in the streaming path, causing more aggressive memory-backed prefetching under hot workloads. Also, a previous alert-suppression tweak silenced host-level RSS alerts for a specific router fleet, delaying detection.
contributing_factors:
- Recent merge (PR #4392) altered buffer cap logic but unit tests did not cover end-to-end streaming memory scenarios.
- Hot prefix skew from a few tenant workloads increased cache churn. Our autoscaler reacted to CPU rather than memory leading to insufficient capacity during memory storms.
- Alert suppression for router RSS to reduce paging noise meant oncall didn't see early warning.
- Clients with aggressive retry behavior amplified reconnect and short-lived session churn.
remediation_and_mitigations:
Short-term (within incident):
- Forced eviction of oversized prefix caches on affected hosts to quickly free memory.
- Autoscaled additional router instances (memory-aware scale-up) for immediate capacity headroom.
- Canary rollback of the buffer-cap regression on 2 canaries; then staged rollout of fixed binary.
Medium-term (24–72h):
- Revert PR #4392's permissive allocation until a full fix with streaming e2e tests lands.
- Tweak KV prefetch throttle defaults for streaming to be conservative under high prefix-skew.
- Re-enable sparse host RSS alerts for streaming routers with higher signal-to-noise using refined thresholds.
Long-term:
- Add an explicit memory-based autoscaling policy for router fleet (scale on RSS and heap percent).
- Build regression e2e test harness that simulates high-concurrency streaming with hot prefix skew.
- Implement per-tenant prefetch budgets to limit a single tenant from dominating cache prefetch resources.

1) Engineering action item: fix buffer accounting and add streaming e2e memory test (owner: Daniel Park, due: 2029-12-20)
2) Ops action item: implement memory-aware autoscaler for router fleet (owner: Priya Menon, due: 2029-12-27)
3) Observability: create composite alert that joins KV cache eviction spikes + streaming stalls (owner: Ethan Li, due: 2029-12-18)

Each action has been entered as JIRA tickets linked above (JIRA-INC-4821 + JIRA-TASK-1256, JIRA-TASK-1257, JIRA-TASK-1258).
lessons_learned:
- Unit and integration tests are necessary but insufficient for streaming runtime changes — we must have a streaming e2e harness that exercises memory under skewed prefixes.
- Memory signals should be first-class for autoscaling and alerting on router fleets that are memory-sensitive.
- Alert suppression needs periodic review; suppressions that reduce signal visibility for critical fleets are higher risk.
- Client retry behavior can magnify incidents; consider client-side recommended backoff and server-side short-lived session protections (rate-limit ephemeral reconnects).
notes_for_runbook:
Add a 'fast rescue' section:
- Step A: identify hosts with RSS > 80% and stream stall counters rising.
- Step B: cordon and drain streamed sessions from one host at a time to avoid mass reconnect storms.
- Step C: run /admin/force-cache-evict --prefix=hot --limit=1000 on affected host; verify memory drop > 20% before uncordoning.
- Step D: if stalls persist, scale router pool memory-capacity by +25% and rollback recent router binary versions.
- Post-incident: capture heap/profile and upload to artifacts store before host reboot.
references: Relevant PRs and dashboards included in linked_artifacts. See grafana panels for kv-eviction-rate, router-rss, streaming-p50-ttfb, live reconnect heatmap. Jira INC and followups track remediation and customer comms.
